nodes.label: The East African (Swahili) coast
nodes.full: Mombasa, Pemba, Kilwa, Zanzibar and the Swahili towns — the overseas theatre into which Oman's Portuguese-inherited empire expands: a source of ivory, gold and enslaved people, the ground of the Zanzibar clove plantations, and eventually the seat to which the Omani capital itself moves.
nodes.src: background — Sheriff, 'Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar' (1987)

nodes.label: British India and the East India Company
nodes.full: After Plassey the Company rules Bengal, and the Gulf becomes the strategic western approach to its Indian empire — a sea lane to be policed, a place for treaties, agents and, by 1809, punitive fleets. The framework of British paramountcy in the Gulf is built from India.
nodes.src: background — Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1795–1880' (1968); Onley, 'The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj' (2007)

nodes.label: Ya'ruba Oman as an Indian Ocean empire
nodes.full: Under Sultan bin Saif I and his successors the Ya'ruba imams used the fleet built to fight the Portuguese to seize their possessions — raiding Diu and Bombay and, after a 33-month siege, taking Mombasa's Fort Jesus in 1698. Oman inherited the Portuguese Swahili coast.
nodes.src: al-Salimi, 'Tuhfat al-Ayan'; Risso, 'Oman and Muscat: An Early Modern History' (1986). Fort Jesus fell in December 1698.

nodes.label: The Ya'ruba civil war and the Persian occupation
nodes.full: Disputed imamates split Oman into the Hinawi and Ghafiri factions and dragged in Nader Shah of Persia, whose troops occupied Muscat and Sohar. The struggle wrecked Ya'rubid legitimacy and left the country to be reunited by whoever could expel the Persians.
nodes.src: Wilkinson, 'The Imamate Tradition of Oman' (1987); the origin of the Hinawi/Ghafiri divide in this war.

nodes.label: Ahmad bin Said founds the Al Bu Said dynasty
nodes.full: Ahmad bin Said, governor of Sohar, drove the Persians out of Oman and was elected imam in 1744. His house has ruled Oman ever since — the oldest continuously reigning dynasty in the Arab world.
nodes.src: al-Salimi; Ibn Ruzayq, 'al-Fath al-Mubin' (history of the Al Bu Said); election of Ahmad bin Said, 1744 (sometimes given 1749).

nodes.label: Sultan bin Ahmad and the Muscat free port
nodes.full: Sultan bin Ahmad — ruling as a secular 'sayyid', not an imam — made Muscat a low-duty free port and the busiest entrepôt of the western Indian Ocean. In 1798 he signed the first British treaty with an Arab Gulf ruler.
nodes.src: Risso (1986); the 1798 qawl-nama with the East India Company. The dropping of the imam title is a constitutional break (Wilkinson 1987).

nodes.label: The Al Sabah become rulers of Kuwait
nodes.full: A section of the Bani Utbah, migrants from Najd, settled the bay of Kuwait around 1716 and by about 1752 had chosen Sabah bin Jaber to handle external affairs and justice — a first-among-equals arrangement with the merchant families that still frames Kuwaiti politics.
nodes.src: Slot, 'The Origins of Kuwait' (1991); the traditional date c.1752 for Sabah I.

nodes.label: The Al Khalifa take Bahrain
nodes.full: The Al Khalifa, another Utbi house, built the pearling port of Zubara on the Qatar coast and in 1783 crossed to conquer Bahrain from its Persian garrison. They have ruled the island ever since — a Sunni dynasty over a largely Shia population.
nodes.src: Slot, 'The Arabs of the Gulf 1602–1784' (1993); the 1783 conquest from Qatar (the 'Battle of Zubara').

nodes.label: The Qawasim maritime power of the lower Gulf
nodes.full: By the late 18th century the Al Qasimi commanded the largest Arab fleet in the Gulf — hundreds of vessels working both shores — and dominated the lower-Gulf carrying trade. Their rivalry with British-protected shipping led Britain to brand the coast 'the Pirate Coast'.
nodes.src: Sultan bin Muhammad al-Qasimi, 'The Myth of Arab Piracy in the Gulf' (1986), the revisionist case; Sultan bin Saqr al-Qasimi ruled from 1803.

nodes.label: The Bani Yas and the founding of Abu Dhabi
nodes.full: The Bani Yas confederation, led by the Al Nahyan of the Al Bu Falah, moved their centre from the Liwa oases to Abu Dhabi island around 1761 after fresh water was found there. Pearling and the date gardens of Liwa sustained the new shaykhdom.
nodes.src: Heard-Bey, 'From Trucial States to United Arab Emirates' (1982); the traditional founding date of Abu Dhabi town, 1761.

nodes.label: The Bani Khalid emirate and the first Saudi state
nodes.full: The Bani Khalid expelled the Ottomans from al-Hasa in 1670 and ruled eastern Arabia for over a century. In 1795 the Wahhabi–Saudi state of Diriyah conquered al-Hasa, absorbing the Gulf's Arabian coast into an expanding religious polity.
nodes.src: Fattah, 'The Politics of Regional Trade in Iraq, Arabia and the Gulf 1745–1900' (1997); the Saudi conquest of al-Hasa, 1795.

nodes.label: The siege of Fort Jesus, Mombasa
nodes.full: Omani forces blockaded and starved the Portuguese garrison of Fort Jesus for nearly three years before storming it. The victory gave Oman the Swahili coast and confirmed it as the dominant power of the western Indian Ocean.
nodes.src: Boxer & de Azevedo, 'Fort Jesus and the Portuguese in Mombasa' (1960); Omani accounts in al-Salimi.

nodes.label: Nader Shah's forces occupy Oman
nodes.full: Invited in by one faction of the Ya'rubid civil war, Nader Shah's army occupied the Omani coast and besieged its forts. Ahmad bin Said's expulsion of the Persians from Sohar and Muscat was the foundation of his claim to rule.
nodes.src: Lockhart, 'Nadir Shah' (1938); Risso (1986). The Persian withdrawal followed Nader Shah's assassination (1747).

nodes.label: The conquest of Bahrain and the wars of Zubara
nodes.full: The Al Khalifa seizure of Bahrain in 1783 set off two decades of war — Persian, Omani and Bani Utbah fleets fighting over the island and its pearl banks, and repeated sieges of the Al Khalifa base at Zubara. The dynasty held on.
nodes.src: Slot (1993); the multi-sided struggle over Bahrain and Zubara, 1780s–1790s.

nodes.label: The Saudi conquest of al-Hasa and the sack of Karbala
nodes.full: The first Saudi state took al-Hasa from the Bani Khalid in 1795 and in 1802 raided the Shia shrine city of Karbala, killing thousands and stripping the tomb of Husayn. Wahhabi power now reached the Gulf coast and alarmed every neighbour.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr, 'Unwan al-Majd fi Tarikh Najd'; the Karbala raid of 1802 (Cole, 'Sacred Space and Holy War', 2002).

nodes.label: Wahhabi pressure on Oman and the occupation of Buraimi
nodes.full: Saudi forces occupied the Buraimi oasis and raided deep into Oman, forcing Sultan bin Ahmad and then Said bin Sultan to pay tribute for years. Oman only shook off the pressure after the first Saudi state was destroyed.
nodes.src: Risso (1986); the Saudi occupation of Buraimi and the Omani tribute (later a source of the 20th-century Buraimi dispute).

nodes.label: The British expeditions against Ras al-Khaimah
nodes.full: The East India Company mounted two naval expeditions against the Qawasim — a raid in 1809–10 and a full campaign in 1819 that captured and demolished Ras al-Khaimah. The second led directly to the treaty that would bind the coast to Britain for 150 years.
nodes.src: The 1809 and 1819 EIC expeditions; the destruction of Ras al-Khaimah (Onley, 'The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj', 2007). Bridges to the Trucial States folio.

nodes.label: Oman abandons the imamate for the sultanate
nodes.full: After Ahmad bin Said, the Al Bu Said stopped seeking election as imams and ruled as hereditary secular princes based on the coast. The Ibadi scholars of the interior never fully accepted this, and the split between a coastal Sultanate and an interior Imamate outlasted the century.
nodes.src: Wilkinson (1987); the coast–interior constitutional divide that culminated in the 20th-century Imamate revolts.

nodes.label: The Kuwaiti merchant compact
nodes.full: Kuwait's pearling and long-distance merchant families delegated defence, justice and foreign dealings to the Al Sabah while keeping control of trade and the town's purse. Ruler and merchants governed as partners — a balance that shaped Kuwait into the modern era.
nodes.src: Slot, 'The Origins of Kuwait' (1991); the ruler–merchant relationship (Crystal, 'Oil and Politics in the Gulf', 1990).

nodes.label: The Muscat customs regime
nodes.full: Muscat charged a flat, low duty on trade and farmed the collection to Hindu merchant financiers, most famously the banian customs-masters. The predictable, light regime is what pulled shipping to Muscat from higher-taxed rivals.
nodes.src: Risso (1986); Allen, 'The Indian merchant community of Masqat', BSOAS 44 (1981).

nodes.label: Wahhabi enforcement in conquered al-Hasa
nodes.full: In the annexed Gulf oases the Saudi state enforced its doctrine — mandatory attendance at prayer, the destruction of tomb-shrines, bans on tobacco and music, and the treatment of the Shia majority as unbelievers. It was the region's first experience of Wahhabi rule.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr, 'Unwan al-Majd'; the enforcement of Wahhabi norms in al-Hasa (Steinberg; Vassiliev, 'The History of Saudi Arabia', 2000).

nodes.label: The 1798 Anglo-Omani treaty
nodes.full: Alarmed by Napoleon in Egypt, the East India Company signed a treaty with Sultan bin Ahmad barring the French and Dutch from Omani ports and stationing a British agent at Muscat. It was the opening move of British paramountcy in the Gulf.
nodes.src: The 1798 qawl-nama and the 1800 supplementary agreement; Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1795–1880' (1968).

nodes.label: The interior ulama reject the Al Bu Said sultanate
nodes.full: To the Ibadi scholars, a hereditary ruler who did not seek election and lived by trade duties on the coast was no imam at all. Their withheld recognition kept alive the idea of a true Imamate in the mountains, ready to be revived.
nodes.src: Wilkinson (1987); the Ibadi juristic critique of Al Bu Said 'kingship'.

nodes.label: The Diriyah pact and the Wahhabi movement
nodes.full: The preacher Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and the amir Muhammad ibn Saud agreed at Diriyah to join religious reform to political power. The doctrine — strict unitarianism, rejection of shrine devotion and Sufism, and the branding of opponents as idolaters — drove a century of expansion.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannam and Ibn Bishr, the Najdi chronicles; ibn Abd al-Wahhab, 'Kitab al-Tawhid'; Commins, 'The Wahhabi Mission and Saudi Arabia' (2006).

nodes.label: The Wahhabi da'wa reaches the Gulf tribes
nodes.full: The Qawasim and other lower-Gulf tribes adopted Wahhabi doctrine and acknowledged Saudi authority, tying the maritime shaykhdoms to the Najdi state. It gave the anti-British struggle on the coast a religious edge.
nodes.src: Kelly (1968); the Qawasim–Saudi alliance around 1800.

nodes.label: Bahrain's Shia majority under a Sunni dynasty
nodes.full: The Al Khalifa conquest placed Bahrain's largely Shia Baharna population under a Sunni ruling house and its tribal followers. The resulting social structure — a Shia agrarian and pearling majority, a Sunni ruling elite — has defined the island's politics ever since.
nodes.src: Cole, IJMES 19 (1987); Khuri, 'Tribe and State in Bahrain' (1980).

nodes.label: The destruction of the shrines
nodes.full: Wahhabi forces demolished domed tombs and shrines wherever they conquered — the shrine of Husayn at Karbala in 1802, Shia sites in the Gulf oases, and the tomb-mosques of Medina after 1805. For Shia and many Sunnis alike it was an assault on the sacred landscape.
nodes.src: Cole, 'Sacred Space and Holy War' (2002); the 1802 Karbala raid and the later demolitions in the Hijaz.

nodes.label: Jabrin Palace
nodes.full: Built by the Ya'rubid imam Bel'arab bin Sultan, Jabrin is the finest Omani palace — a fortified house with painted wooden ceilings, carved doorways, a Quran school and cool date-store rooms. It is the high point of Ya'rubid domestic architecture.
nodes.src: Jabrin (Jabreen) Castle; Omani Ministry of Heritage; Damluji, 'The Architecture of Oman' (1998).

nodes.label: The great round tower of Nizwa Fort
nodes.full: Sultan bin Saif I raised a squat drum tower 36 metres across and 30 high over Nizwa, purpose-built to mount and withstand cannon. It is the emblem of Ya'rubid Oman and one of the largest fort towers in Arabia.
nodes.src: Nizwa Fort; construction under Sultan bin Saif I; Damluji (1998).

nodes.label: At-Turaif — the mud-brick capital of the first Saudi state
nodes.full: The at-Turaif quarter of Diriyah, with its palaces, mosque and defensive walls in the ornamented Najdi mud-brick style, was the seat of the first Saudi state until an Egyptian army razed it in 1818. Its ruins are now a World Heritage Site.
nodes.src: At-Turaif District in ad-Dir'iyah, UNESCO World Heritage (2010).

nodes.label: The sea music of the pearling fleet
nodes.full: The 18th-century pearling boom fixed the genres of Gulf sea music — the fjiri sung by returning crews, the nahham's work-chants, the drums and hand-clapping of the port. It is a living tradition whose social root is the labour of this period.
nodes.src: Gulf pearling music (fjiri / fann al-bahr); documented from the late 19th century (al-Khan; Rovsing Olsen, 'Music in Bahrain', 2002).

nodes.label: The Omani khanjar and Gulf silver
nodes.full: The curved khanjar dagger with its silver-wired sheath became the mark of an Omani man of standing, and Gulf silversmiths — many of them from the Shia oases — produced jewellery and vessels traded across Arabia and East Africa.
nodes.src: Omani silver and the khanjar (Hawley, 'Omani Silver', 1978); the silversmithing traditions of Nizwa and al-Hasa.

nodes.label: The Omani juristic compilations
nodes.full: Ya'rubid and post-Ya'rubid scholars gathered Ibadi law and history into large compilations — the 'Bayan al-Shar', the works of al-Salimi's predecessors — preserving a legal tradition that the interior would use to judge, and reject, the coastal rulers.
nodes.src: The Omani 'siyar' and fiqh compilations; Wilkinson, 'Ibâdism' (2010).

nodes.label: Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's Kitab al-Tawhid
nodes.full: The founding text of the Wahhabi movement argues that most professed Muslims had lapsed into idolatry through saint-veneration and intercession, and that restoring pure monotheism justified war against them. Its ideas reshaped religious life across the Gulf's Arabian coast.
nodes.src: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, 'Kitab al-Tawhid'; Commins, 'The Wahhabi Mission and Saudi Arabia' (2006).

nodes.label: Carsten Niebuhr's survey of the Gulf
nodes.full: The sole survivor of the Danish Arabia expedition, Niebuhr mapped the Gulf, described Muscat's trade and government, listed the tribes and shaykhdoms, and recorded Bahrain's pearl fishery — the first modern scientific account of the region.
nodes.src: Carsten Niebuhr, 'Reisebeschreibung nach Arabien und andern umliegenden Ländern' (1774–78); 'Beschreibung von Arabien' (1772).

nodes.label: The Najdi and Omani dynastic chronicles
nodes.full: Ibn Ghannam and Ibn Bishr wrote year-by-year histories of the Saudi state; Omani scholars chronicled the Ya'ruba and Al Bu Said. For the first time both the Najdi interior and Oman produced their own running historical record of the period as it happened.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannam, 'Rawdat al-Afkar'; Ibn Bishr, 'Unwan al-Majd fi Tarikh Najd'; the Omani chronicle tradition later synthesised by Ibn Ruzayq and al-Salimi.

nodes.label: Muscat, entrepôt of the western Indian Ocean
nodes.full: At its peak Muscat re-exported the goods of India, the Gulf, Arabia and East Africa through one low-duty harbour, its bazaars worked by Kutchi Hindus, Khoja Ismailis, Jews and Arab merchants. It was the freest and busiest port the Gulf had seen for centuries.
nodes.src: Risso (1986); the Muscat trade figures and merchant communities (Allen 1981).

nodes.label: The 18th-century pearl boom
nodes.full: Rising Indian and European demand drove the greatest pearling expansion the Gulf had known. Kuwait went from a watering-place to a town of hundreds of boats; Zubara and the Trucial ports grew on pearl money; the fishery became the coast's economic engine.
nodes.src: Carter, 'Sea of Pearls' (2012); the 18th-century growth of the pearling towns.

nodes.label: Kuwait, the port of the desert
nodes.full: When plague and Persian occupation crippled Basra in the 1770s, Kuwait took over as the Gulf terminus of the great desert caravan route to Aleppo, and its merchant fleet carried Basra dates and Indian goods. Neutrality and low costs made it the trade's safe harbour.
nodes.src: Slot, 'The Origins of Kuwait' (1991); Kuwait's boom during the 1775–79 Persian occupation of Basra.

nodes.label: The Omani East African trade
nodes.full: From the Swahili coast Oman drew ivory, gold, gum copal and, increasingly, enslaved people, exchanged for Indian cloth and Gulf dates. Under Said bin Sultan the first clove plantations were laid out on Zanzibar — the beginning of a plantation economy worked by slaves.
nodes.src: Sheriff, 'Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar' (1987); the growth of the Omani–East African trade.

nodes.label: The Qawasim carrying trade
nodes.full: The Qawasim fleet carried pearls, dates, dried fish and re-exported Indian goods along both Gulf shores and beyond. British accounts recast this competition as piracy; the ships were doing the same work every Gulf merchant marine did.
nodes.src: al-Qasimi, 'The Myth of Arab Piracy in the Gulf' (1986); the commercial rivalry underlying the 'piracy' charge.

nodes.label: The ocean-going dhow yards of Sur and Kuwait
nodes.full: Gulf shipwrights built the large baghlah and ghanjah traders that carried Oman's empire and Kuwait's commerce across the ocean, and the nimble bum and sambuk for the coasting and pearling trades. Sur and Kuwait were the great building centres.
nodes.src: Agius, 'Classic Ships of Islam' (2008) and 'In the Wake of the Dhow' (2002); the Sur and Kuwait shipbuilding traditions.

nodes.label: The Omani cannon fort
nodes.full: The Ya'ruba covered Oman with forts designed around artillery — thick round towers, gun galleries, date-syrup 'murder holes', deep wells and falaj channels to withstand siege. Al-Hazm castle, roofed in solid stone, is the extreme case.
nodes.src: Damluji, 'The Architecture of Oman' (1998); Al-Hazm Castle (c.1711).

nodes.label: The pearling rig and its division of labour
nodes.full: Gulf pearling was a refined technology: the nose-clip, leather finger-guards, a stone weight to sink the diver and a rope for the hauler to pull him up, worked in pairs on boats crewed to a fixed roster of diver, hauler, captain and apprentice.
nodes.src: Villiers, 'Sons of Sinbad' (1940); Carter, 'Sea of Pearls' (2012), on the diving technology and crew organisation.

nodes.label: Falaj restoration under the Ya'ruba
nodes.full: The Ya'rubid peace let Oman rebuild and extend the aflaj wrecked in earlier wars, and the agricultural surplus funded the forts and the fleet. Water engineering and sea power were two ends of the same prosperity.
nodes.src: Wilkinson, 'Water and Tribal Settlement in South-East Arabia' (1977); the Ya'rubid agricultural revival.

nodes.label: Oman rules the Swahili coast
nodes.full: After Fort Jesus fell, Omani governors held the East African ports, though Mombasa's Mazrui governors soon went their own way. Under Said bin Sultan the Omani presence deepened toward the move of the capital itself to Zanzibar in 1840.
nodes.src: Sheriff, 'Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar' (1987); the Mazrui of Mombasa and their break from Muscat.

nodes.label: The Bani Utbah migration to the coast
nodes.full: Over three generations sections of the Bani Utbah moved from the Najdi interior to the Gulf, founding Kuwait, building Zubara in Qatar and finally conquering Bahrain. One tribal migration seeded three of today's Gulf ruling houses.
nodes.src: Slot, 'The Origins of Kuwait' (1991) and 'The Arabs of the Gulf 1602–1784' (1993).

nodes.label: Britain enters Gulf diplomacy
nodes.full: The French threat after 1798 turned the East India Company from a trading presence into a diplomatic power in the Gulf — treaties with Muscat, a resident agent, and by 1809 warships acting against rulers it deemed hostile. The framework of British paramountcy was being laid.
nodes.src: Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1795–1880' (1968); Onley, 'The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj' (2007).

nodes.label: The Dutch on Kharg and the French at Muscat
nodes.full: Other Europeans probed the Gulf too — the Dutch built a fort on Kharg island under Baron Kniphausen in the 1750s, and French agents courted Muscat during the revolutionary wars. Britain's eventual dominance was not a foregone conclusion.
nodes.src: Floor, 'The Persian Gulf: The Rise and Fall of Bandar-e Lengeh' and 'Dutch–Persian relations'; the Kharg episode (1753–66).

nodes.label: Indian merchant capital in the Gulf
nodes.full: Hindu and Khoja merchant houses from Kutch and Sindh financed Gulf trade, farmed the customs of Muscat and Bahrain, and lent to the rulers themselves. Gulf commerce ran on Indian credit long before it ran on British power.
nodes.src: Allen, 'The Indian merchant community of Masqat', BSOAS 44 (1981); Onley on the banian networks of the Gulf ports.

nodes.label: The fall of Safavid Persia
nodes.full: An Afghan army sacked Isfahan and ended effective Safavid rule. The collapse of authority on the Persian shore let Arab tribes — the Al Khalifa on Bahrain, the Qawasim on the Persian coast, the Bani Ka'b in Arabistan — carve out maritime power.
nodes.src: Axworthy, 'The Sword of Persia' (2006); the effect of Safavid collapse on the Arab Gulf shaykhdoms.

nodes.label: Nader Shah and a Persian navy on the Gulf
nodes.full: Nader Shah briefly rebuilt Persian power, invaded Oman and assembled a Gulf fleet with Indian-bought ships and Omani shipwrights. His assassination in 1747 collapsed the project and threw both shores back into a scramble of local powers.
nodes.src: Lockhart, 'Nadir Shah' (1938); Floor, 'The Persian Gulf: A Political and Economic History' (2006), on Nader's navy.

nodes.label: The East India Company becomes a power in India
nodes.full: After Plassey the Company turned from merchant to ruler in India, and the Gulf became the strategic western approach to its new empire — a sea lane and a listening post to be controlled rather than merely traded in.
nodes.src: the transformation of the EIC (Bayly, 'Indian Society and the Making of the British Empire', 1988); the Gulf's new strategic role.

nodes.label: Napoleon in Egypt
nodes.full: The French occupation of Egypt raised the spectre of an overland threat to British India and triggered the first British treaties in the Gulf. A European war fought on the Nile redrew the Gulf's diplomatic map.
nodes.src: Napoleon's Egyptian expedition (1798–1801) and its knock-on effect on British Gulf policy (Kelly 1968).

nodes.label: Muhammad Ali destroys the first Saudi state
nodes.full: On the Ottoman sultan's orders, Muhammad Ali of Egypt sent armies that retook the Hijaz and, in 1818, stormed and levelled Diriyah, executing the last Saudi amir in Istanbul. Wahhabi pressure on the Gulf eased — for a generation.
nodes.src: Vassiliev, 'The History of Saudi Arabia' (2000); the fall of Diriyah, 1818.

nodes.label: The Qajars take Persia
nodes.full: The Qajar dynasty reunified Persia and claimed its Gulf coast, but ruled the south weakly through tax-farming governors. For most of the next century the Arab shaykhdoms of both shores dealt with Britain, not Tehran.
nodes.src: the Qajar consolidation (Amanat, 'Iran: A Modern History', 2017); Persian weakness on the southern coast.

nodes.label: The pearl diver's debt
nodes.full: Divers took a cash advance (the salaf) from their boat captain against the season's catch and rarely cleared it. The debt was carried year to year and passed to sons — a system of hereditary bondage that tied the labour force to the fleet.
nodes.src: Carter, 'Sea of Pearls' (2012); the salaf/advance system and its critics (later the 1930s reforms).

nodes.label: Slavery on the Omani coast
nodes.full: Enslaved East Africans worked as pearl divers, sailors, date-garden labour, domestic servants and soldiers across the Omani world, and in growing numbers on the new Zanzibar clove plantations. The trade was central to the coast's economy, not incidental to it.
nodes.src: Sheriff, 'Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar' (1987); Lodhi and others on Omani-era East African slavery.

nodes.label: Women and the household economy of the dive season
nodes.full: With the men at sea for four months every summer, women ran the pearling towns — managing money and provisions on credit, holding property, and keeping the household solvent against the uncertain return. The pearl economy depended on this unpaid onshore work.
nodes.src: al-Mughni, 'Women in Kuwait' (2001); the gendered division of the pearling year.

nodes.label: The Hinawi–Ghafiri divide
nodes.full: The factional split that began in the Ya'rubid civil war hardened into two named blocs — Hinawi and Ghafiri — that cut across tribes and villages and structured every Omani conflict for the next two centuries. It was a social fault line the state had to manage rather than heal.
nodes.src: Wilkinson (1987); the Hinawi/Ghafiri alignment in Omani society.

nodes.label: Same-sex roles on the Omani–Swahili coast
nodes.full: The plantation-slavery world Oman built on the East African coast trafficked boys and youths for domestic and sexual service alongside women, and Swahili coastal society carried a socially recognised role — later documented as the shoga, and named hanithi straight from the Arabic khanith — of men understood as receptive partners who did women's ritual work at weddings. The category moved along the same Indian Ocean routes as the khanith of the Omani coast and the mukhannath before it.
nodes.src: Direct evidence for the Omani period is sparse; the picture is reconstructed from 19th- and 20th-century sources. Richard Burton's writings on the East African coast and his 'Terminal Essay' (1885) — whose 'Sotadic Zone' is a Victorian orientalist theory, not a neutral observation. G. Shepherd, 'Rank, Gender, and Homosexuality: Mombasa as a Key to Understanding Sexual Options', in Caplan (ed.), 'The Cultural Construction of Sexuality' (1987). The Swahili term 'hanithi' derives from Arabic 'khanith'. Zanzibar slavery and concubinage: A. Sheriff, 'Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar' (1987).
